title: Second Epilogue — Chapter 2
paragraphs: Historians who write biographies, or histories of a single nation, understand this force as a power built into heroes and rulers. In their telling, events happen purely by the will of a Napoleon, an Alexander, or whichever figure they are writing about. Ask this kind of historian what force makes events happen, and the answer satisfies only so long as there is just one historian to each event. As soon as historians of different nationalities and different leanings start describing the same event, their answers immediately lose all meaning. Each of them understands this force not merely differently from the others, but often in flatly contradictory ways. One historian says an event was produced by Napoleon's power, another that it was produced by Alexander's, a third that it came from the power of some other person entirely. What is more, historians of this kind contradict one another even on the question of what a given person's authority rested on. Thiers, a Bonapartist, says Napoleon's power rested on his virtue and his genius. Lanfrey, a Republican, says it rested on his trickery and his deception of the people. So historians of this class, by tearing down each other's positions, tear down any understanding of the force that produces events, and give no answer at all to history's essential question.

Writers of universal history, who deal with all nations at once, seem to recognize how mistaken the specialist historians' view of the force producing events really is. They do not treat it as a power built into heroes and rulers, but as the resultant of many forces pushing in different directions—the single outcome they all add up to. In describing a war, or the subjugation of a people, a general historian looks for the cause of the event not in the power of one man, but in the interaction of the many people connected to that event.

On this view, the power of historical figures is presented as the product of many forces, and can no longer, it would seem, be treated as a force that itself produces events. And yet in most cases the universal historians still use the idea of power as a force that produces events in its own right, and treat it as their cause. In their accounts, a historical figure is first the product of his era, his power merely the resultant of various forces—and then his power turns into a force producing events all by itself. Gervinus, Schlosser, and others, for instance, at one point prove that Napoleon was a product of the Revolution, of the ideas of 1789 and so on. At another point they flatly state that the campaign of 1812, and other things they disapprove of, were simply the product of Napoleon's misguided will. They also say that the very ideas of 1789 were stopped in their development by Napoleon's whim. The ideas of the Revolution and the general temper of the age produced Napoleon's power. But Napoleon's power suppressed the ideas of the Revolution and the general temper of the age.

This curious contradiction is not an accident. Not only does it turn up at every step, but the universal historians' accounts are made up, from end to end, of a chain of just such contradictions. It happens because once the universal historians enter the field of analysis, they stop halfway.

To break a composite, or resultant, force down into the component forces that equal it, those components must add up to the resultant. The universal historians never observe this condition. So, to explain the resultant forces, they are obliged to bring in—alongside their insufficient components—some other, unexplained force acting on the outcome.

Specialist historians describing the campaign of 1813, or the restoration of the Bourbons, state plainly that these events were produced by Alexander's will. But the universal historian Gervinus, refuting this view of the specialist historians, tries to show that the campaign of 1813 and the restoration of the Bourbons were due to other things besides Alexander's will—to the activity of Stein, Metternich, Madame de Staël, Talleyrand, Fichte, Chateaubriand, and others. The historian, in effect, breaks Alexander's power down into its components: Talleyrand, Chateaubriand, and the rest. But the sum of those components—that is, the interactions among Chateaubriand, Talleyrand, Madame de Staël, and the others—plainly does not equal the resultant, which is the fact of millions of Frenchmen submitting to the Bourbons. That Chateaubriand, Madame de Staël, and the others said certain words to one another affected only their own mutual relations; it does not account for the submission of millions. And so the historian still has to explain how the submission of millions of people could result from these relations of theirs—how, that is, component forces adding up to one A could give a resultant equal to a thousand times A. To do it he is obliged to fall back once more on power, the very force he had denied, and to treat it as the resultant of the forces. Which is to say, he has to admit an unexplained force acting on the resultant. And that is exactly what the universal historians do, and as a result they contradict not only the specialist historians but themselves.

Peasants have no clear idea of what causes rain. Depending on whether they want rain or fine weather, they say: "The wind has blown the clouds away," or, "The wind has brought up the clouds." In just the same way, the universal historians sometimes, when it suits them and fits their theory, say that power is the result of events, and sometimes, when they want to prove something else, say that power produces events.

A third class of historians—the so-called historians of culture—take that force to be something different again. They follow the path laid down by the universal historians, who sometimes accept writers and ladies as forces producing events. They see that force in what is called culture—in mental activity.

The historians of culture are quite consistent with their forerunners, the writers of universal history. If historical events can be explained by the fact that certain people treated one another in such and such ways, why not explain them by the fact that such and such people wrote such and such books? Out of the immense number of signs that accompany every living phenomenon, these historians pick out the sign of intellectual activity and declare that this sign is the cause. But despite all their efforts to prove that the cause of events lies in intellectual activity, only by a great stretch can one admit that there is any connection at all between intellectual activity and the movement of peoples. And in no case can one admit that intellectual activity controls people's actions. That view is not confirmed by such facts as the very cruel murders of the French Revolution, which came out of the doctrine of the equality of man, or the very cruel wars and executions that came out of the preaching of love.

But even granting as correct every one of the cleverly devised arguments these histories are filled with—even granting that nations are governed by some undefined force called an idea—history's essential question still goes unanswered. To the old power of monarchs, and to the influence of advisers and other people brought in by the universal historians, another and newer force is now added—the idea—and its connection with the masses needs explaining. It is possible to understand that Napoleon had power, and so events occurred; with some effort one may even conceive that Napoleon, together with other influences, was the cause of an event. But how a book, Le Contrat Social, had the effect of making Frenchmen begin to drown one another cannot be understood without an explanation of how this new force is causally linked to the event.

Undoubtedly some relation exists among all who live at the same time, and so it is possible to find some connection between men's intellectual activity and their historical movements—just as such a connection may be found between the movements of humanity and commerce, handicraft, gardening, or anything else you please. But why intellectual activity in particular should be treated by the historians of culture as the cause, or the expression, of the whole historical movement is hard to understand. Only the following considerations can have led the historians to such a conclusion. (1) History is written by learned men, and so it is natural and agreeable for them to think that the activity of their own class supplies the basis of the movement of all humanity—just as a similar belief is natural and agreeable to traders, farmers, and soldiers. If traders and soldiers do not say so, that is merely because they do not write history. (2) Spiritual activity, enlightenment, civilization, culture, ideas: these are all indistinct, indefinite conceptions, and under their banner it is very easy to use words with a still less definite meaning, words that can therefore be readily worked into any theory.

But set aside the intrinsic quality of histories of this kind (which may possibly even be of use to someone for something). What makes the histories of culture significant—and all general histories are coming more and more to resemble them—is this. They examine various religious, philosophic, and political doctrines seriously and minutely as the causes of events. Then, the moment they have to describe an actual historical event, such as the campaign of 1812, they involuntarily describe it as resulting from an exercise of power, and say plainly that it was the result of Napoleon's will. Speaking so, the historians of culture involuntarily contradict themselves, and show that the new force they have devised does not account for what happens in history, and that history can only be explained by introducing a power they apparently do not recognize.
